findings.statement: CXCR2 ranks first in the convergence ranking, with phase II and III CXCR1 and CXCR2 antagonists (reparixin, navarixin, ladarixin, SX-682) listed in Open Targets, yet the verbatim-checked relation set has no CXCR2 relation. Literature support is limited to titles and sentences from a Mendelian randomization/colocalization study that names CXCR1 and CXCR2 as neutrophil-extracellular-trap-related treatment targets in UC, and an eQTL/pQTL/transcriptome study of the CXCL5/CXCR2 axis in neutrophil chemotaxis. PubTator3 (machine-extracted) links CXCR2 to UC in several publications.

The axis of CXCL8 with CXCR1 and CXCR2 is reported to participate in UC pathogenesis through PI3K/Akt, MAPK and NF-kappaB signalling; CXCL8 was also a PPI hub gene in a bioinformatic study and showed diagnostic performance in blood RNA-seq validation for IBD. PXR is proposed to inhibit CXCL8 expression (speculative). Support is mostly bioinformatic or review-level, with no prospective biomarker validation in this corpus.

A single study (PMID:40370742) reports IDO1 elevated in UC patients and correlated with M1 macrophage polarization, with IDO1 inducing M1 polarization through the ER stress GRP78-XBP1 pathway; the inhibitor methyl-tryptophan ameliorated DSS colitis. Evidence is one paper with a mouse model; no human trial of IDO1 inhibition in UC is in the corpus, although IDO1 inhibitors exist in oncology.

MMP1 is a bioinformatic hub gene and was reported with strong diagnostic potential in a UC-associated CRC signature, with ilomastat only a docking-predicted inhibitor. MMP1 and MMP3, S100A8 and IL1B transcripts modified by mirikizumab correlate with Mayo, Geboes and Robarts indices, supporting use as pharmacodynamic activity markers rather than a validated target.

CHI3L1 is upregulated in UC patients and correlates with NLRP3 inflammasome expression; in preclinical work CHI3L1 promotes macrophage pyroptosis via BCAT1/NF-kappaB and its inhibition is protective. Velpatasvir binding to recombinant CHI3L1 was confirmed in vitro by microscale thermophoresis. It has no approved drug in Open Targets; evidence is preclinical.

DUOX2 is among the most elevated proteins in inflamed UC biopsies versus healthy controls, shares upregulation across IBD and CRC, and is proposed as a candidate biomarker. A herbal formula (TLXDS) alleviated UC by inhibiting DUOX2 and ferroptosis, but this is a single preclinical study and DUOX2 has no drug listed.

AQP9 is predominantly expressed in neutrophils; one study reports it promotes NET formation through JAK2-STAT3-mediated pyroptosis and aggravates epithelial injury in UC, and another confirmed its overexpression in DSS and anti-CD40 colitis models. The signal is therefore neutrophil-derived infiltrate rather than epithelial change, and it has no drugs.

S100A9 expression is described as performing excellently for diagnosing active UC, and calprotectin (S100A8/S100A9) transcripts associate with endoscopic disease. In a tofacitinib single-cell study S100A9 was upregulated with IL1B, IL6, CXCL1 and CXCL8 in non-responders, and a response was associated with its downregulation in resident macrophages, suggesting a link to treatment non-response.

CXCL1 is nominated as a diagnostic or activity marker in several bioinformatic and machine-learning studies, but with only modest individual discrimination in at least one; it is not a validated clinical marker. The corpus also links it to the Th1 IFN-gamma mechanism of electroacupuncture.

IL1B is listed among credible diagnostic and therapeutic biomarkers for UC, and rises with IL6, CXCL1, CXCL8 and S100A9 after tofacitinib in non-responders, which makes it a candidate non-response marker. No IL-1 blockade evidence in UC is in the verbatim relations despite approved IL-1 drugs for other indications.

SLC26A3 is reported significantly lower in UC by ONT RNA-seq. It is downregulated in expression and also has genetic association in Open Targets, but only a single literature relation exists, so the literature is thin for a gene with convergent genetic and expression support.

HMGCS2 is decreased in UC patients in two studies, one reporting high diagnostic value. This is the epithelial metabolic-loss side of the signature, supported only by bioinformatic and small validation studies.

LCN2 is upregulated in UC and IBD and reported as a diagnostic biomarker for UC-associated carcinogenesis, with expression higher in short-duration UC than in long-duration UC and UC-associated cancer, so it behaves as an activity marker that falls with disease duration.

CD274 (PD-L1) was called a hub gene associated with UC and macrophage infiltration in one bioinformatic study, and PD-L1 was validated by immunohistochemistry in a Japanese cohort; CBX3 limits IFN-gamma/STAT1/PD-L1 signalling in colon epithelium. Approved PD-L1 antibodies exist for oncology but no UC therapeutic evidence is in the corpus, and the verbatim-checked relation set is empty for this gene.

caveats: Several top-ranked genes (CXCR2, CXCR1, CD274, FCGR2A, JAK2, IL2RA, TREM1, INHBA, CXCL5, S100A12, PI3, REG1A, CDH3) have no verbatim-checked literature relations in this corpus, although they score high via Open Targets and expression; I searched or queried only a subset of them.
Most literature relations are bioinformatic hub-gene or signature studies (GEO, machine learning) and preclinical mouse models; none is a randomized trial of the gene as a target.
CXCR2 statements rely on chunk sentences and machine-extracted PubTator3 relations, not on verbatim-checked relations.
Many upregulated genes (AQP9, S100A8/9, CXCL8, LCN2, IDO1) are neutrophil or myeloid-derived, so their signal may reflect infiltrating immune cells rather than epithelial change.
No numeric values are cited in these statements, so no numeric claims are listed.
